Today's treatments act more bluntly, across the whole body. And because the brain uses similar molecular machinery to learn rewards from many drugs, the answer could reach further. It might help with other addictions and with compulsive behaviors too.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is a funded plan, not a finding. The project has just begun, and the source reports no results yet. Whether mitochondria drive nicotine-seeking is the question being tested. Any new treatment would come only if the research succeeds, and after much more work.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Craving may be written not only in how brain cells connect, but in how each cell powers and runs itself.

recall.q: Why does Calarco think mitochondria could matter for addiction, beyond giving neurons energy?
recall.a: Mitochondria also shape how neurons talk to each other, help cells read genes and build proteins, and help make steroid hormones. So if nicotine changes them, it could change how reward neurons learn. Finding the exact pathways that go wrong could lead to drugs that target that problem more precisely than today's treatments.

cards.title: Randy Weston: raised as an African born in America
cards.body: The jazz pianist Randy Weston reached Morocco in 1967, but Africa was not new to him. His father had prepared him for years. He hung portraits of African kings on a café wall and taught history lessons meant to undo the Tarzan movies. Later, jazz taught him the same lesson.

sections.text:
In a small luncheonette in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn, the walls were covered with portraits of African kings. The place was called the Panama Café, and musicians and teachers sat at its tables. The owner was Frank Weston. His son Randy was born one hundred years ago, and he grew up to be a jazz pianist.

Frank wanted his son to see himself as "an African born in America." He followed the Pan-African ideas of Marcus Garvey. Pan-Africanism is the belief that Black people everywhere share one heritage and should stand together. Frank also had a clear enemy: the Tarzan movies of Randy's childhood, which showed Africa as a wild jungle. So he taught a different history. He taught ancient Egypt and ancient Ethiopia. He taught the great university of Fes in Morocco. He taught the Moors, the North African Muslims who ruled much of Spain. In this story, Africa was not the backward place. Africa was the teacher.

The lessons went on outside the home. Street-corner teachers such as John Henrik Clarke and Yosef Ben-Jochannan, known as Dr. Ben, deepened Randy's Afrocentrism. Afrocentrism is a way of reading history that puts Africa at the center, not at the edge.

Then music did the same work. As a young pianist, Weston was deeply moved by the way Duke Ellington brought Africa into his Liberian Suite of 1948. In the early 1950s, he played piano for the jazz historian Marshall Stearns at the Music Inn, a cultural center in the Berkshires. Stearns would talk, then play, tracing jazz back to the Caribbean and West Africa. He showed three roots. The first was polyrhythm: several rhythms played at once. The second was call and response: one voice calls and others answer. The third was improvisation: making music up in the moment. This broke a tired story that Weston liked to mock: that jazz simply came "up the river from New Orleans," as if it were born only in America.

So in April 1967, Weston arrived in Tangier, Morocco. He had just finished a US State Department tour of fourteen African countries and Lebanon. He was not meeting Africa for the first time. A café wall, some street-corner teachers and the roots of his own music had been preparing him for years. Identity, it seems, can be taught long before it is lived.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: In this story, Africa was not the backward place. Africa was the teacher.

recall.q: How did Randy Weston come to feel African before he ever went to Africa, and which false story did each influence push against?
recall.a: His father taught him about Egypt, Ethiopia, Fes and the Moors to push back against the Tarzan picture of Africa as a wild jungle. Later, Marshall Stearns traced jazz back to West African and Caribbean roots such as polyrhythm and call and response. That pushed back against the idea that jazz was born only in New Orleans.

cards.title: Enemy feminisms: when your own movement has opponents
cards.body: When someone in a movement does something bad, we often say they were never a real member. But feminism has no membership card. The theorist Sophie Lewis offers another view: some people are feminists and still on the other side.

sections.text:
Gloria Steinem died earlier this month. Her obituaries quickly split into two camps. In one, she is the great feminist icon, the face of the movement. In the other, she is a false feminist. To these writers, she shows the limits of the Second Wave, the name for that earlier stage of feminism. Some even suggest she betrayed the movement for the CIA.

The writer Amelia Horgan, in Tribune, uses this split to look at a common habit. Political movements are always drawing their borders. Sometimes a person acting in the movement's name does something questionable, or even reactionary, meaning it pushes things backward. The usual reply: they can't really be one of us, because no real comrade would do that.

Horgan does not call this reply wrong. But it usually describes what the movement should be and how its members ought to act. It does not describe what the movement is, or what it has been. It is an ideal, not a head count.

The problem is that feminism is not a club. Anyone can call themselves a feminist. Others can disagree, but nobody can take the word away. So the real question is what to do when someone fails your own standards. Horgan's standards, for example, are anti-imperialist and anti-capitalist.

The feminist theorist Sophie Lewis has an answer. Such people are not outside the movement. Lewis calls what they stand for "enemy feminisms". They are still feminist, because they fight limits that a male-dominated order puts on people. But their politics are not ours.

Notice what Lewis does not say. She does not say these people are outside the movement. This moves the fight. You stop arguing over who owns the label. Instead you can say plainly: this is feminism, and I oppose it.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Sometimes the honest answer is not "they're not one of us" but "they're one of us, and I'm against them."

recall.q: What does Sophie Lewis mean by "enemy feminisms", and how is that different from saying someone is not a real feminist?
recall.a: Lewis says people whose politics we reject can still be feminists, because they fight limits a male-dominated order puts on people. So you don't deny them the label. You admit they are feminists and oppose them anyway.
